fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces the target refractory Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W composition-screening strategy with carbon-assisted precipitation processing of CoCrFeMnNi, so it does not reconstruct the target material, intervention, or test conditions.

The claim that 0.1–0.3 wt% carbon and a dilute nano-carbide population will measurably increase bulk Young’s modulus is not adequately justified; precipitation generally changes strength much more than elastic modulus.

The cited evidence concerns different alloy chemistries and mechanisms and does not establish the proposed carbide-forming heat treatment in CoCrFeMnNi or simultaneous improvements in modulus, ductility, and fracture toughness.
explanation: This is a testable and broadly relevant structural-HEA hypothesis, but it is a different strategy from the hidden target. The target used validated composition-based modulus estimates and VEC screening to select Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5, followed by room-temperature compression of the as-cast alloy; the generated proposal instead invokes thermomechanical processing and nano-carbides in a Cantor alloy. Its precipitation-strengthening premise is plausible, and it recognizes precipitate coarsening as a boundary, but simultaneous gains in strength, ductility, fracture resistance, and especially Young’s modulus are not supported by the supplied evidence. The baseline lacks quantified properties and matched carbon-only, forging-only, and aging-only controls. The experiment could assess the proposal, but the falsification criterion does not specify a modulus threshold and combines several processing variables, making causal discrimination incomplete. The approach is also established rather than notably novel.
